name: Rotation halts cylindrical collapse
description: A cylindrical shell of counterrotating dust with a lower bound on its circumference set by particle angular momentum and mass per proper length.
convention: We use $G = c = 1$, with times, radii, and the axial coordinate carrying dimensions of length and $\phi$ dimensionless. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
history: A cylindrical shell can have zero total angular momentum while every particle in it circles the axis. Half of the dust moves in each direction, with angular momentum per unit rest mass of magnitude $\alpha$. Theocharis A. Apostolatos and Kip S. Thorne wrote in their 1992 abstract that "an infinitesimal amount of rotation can halt the general relativistic gravitational collapse of a pressure-free cylindrical body" [apostolatos1992rotation]. Their lower bound is $C \geq 8\pi\alpha\Lambda$, where $C$ is the circumference and $\Lambda$ is the rest mass per unit proper length along the shell.¶The axial length changes with the gravitational field, so $\Lambda$ can change during the motion. The conserved rest mass per unit axial Killing coordinate is $\lambda$; if the axial length factor is $e^{\psi_\Sigma}$, then $\Lambda = \lambda e^{-\psi_\Sigma}$. The circumferential radius is $R e^{-\psi_\Sigma}$, and the same bound becomes $R \geq 4\alpha\lambda$ [apostolatos1992rotation]. This is a universal lower bound within their cylindrical shell model; the turning radius also depends on the initial motion and gravitational waves.¶The shell joins two cylindrical vacuum regions, each admitting gravitational waves. Its particles supply a surface energy density and an azimuthal stress, with zero stress along the axis. The two sides agree on distances measured within the shell; their extrinsic curvatures differ by the surface stress [gleiser2012radiative]. The oppositely moving streams cancel the angular momentum flux and add their azimuthal stresses.¶Flat space fills the interior of the static equilibrium shell, whose exterior is a static cylindrical vacuum. Reinaldo J. Gleiser and Marcos A. Ramirez also constructed dynamical solutions with a flat interior and a radiating exterior [gleiser2012radiative]. For general motion, gravitational waves can enter the interior, and its curvature evolves with the shell. A spherical shell has no such coupling, since spherical symmetry removes vacuum gravitational radiation.¶With a regular axis, the interior wave energy constrains the radial metric coefficient. Together with the positive lapse on each side and the shell's matching condition, this constraint implies $R > 4\alpha\lambda$ at regular points of the evolution. At $\alpha = 0$ the positive lower bound vanishes. Fernando Echeverria followed a cylindrical dust shell released from rest and found collapse to a naked singularity in finite time, accompanied by a burst of gravitational waves [echeverria1993cylindrical].

related.text: The shell at equilibrium has a static cylindrical vacuum exterior. Its mass and particle angular momentum fix the exterior parameters through the matching conditions [gleiser2012radiative].
Cylindrical gravitational waves occupy the vacuum outside the moving shell. Their boundary data are coupled to the shell by its surface stress [gleiser2012radiative].

Both constructions support dust through particle angular momentum with vanishing bulk rotation. The cluster distributes particles through a sphere; the cylinder concentrates them on a shell and admits vacuum gravitational radiation [gleiser2012radiative].

Both shells evolve through the jump in extrinsic curvature across a material surface. The spherical dust shell has zero tangential stress; the cylindrical shell carries the azimuthal stress of its orbiting particles [gleiser2012radiative].

coordinates.name: Cylindrical Interior

parameters.description: Dimensionless cylindrical wave amplitude; the vacuum wave equation is $\partial_t^2\psi = \partial_\rho^2\psi + \partial_\rho\psi/\rho$. The restricted flat interior has $\psi = \gamma = 0$.

Dimensionless radial function satisfying $\partial_\rho\gamma = \rho((\partial_\rho\psi)^2 + (\partial_t\psi)^2)$ and $\partial_t\gamma = 2\rho\,\partial_\rho\psi\,\partial_t\psi$. A regular axis has $\gamma(t,0)=0$.
Canonical radius of the shell at the regional time $t$; its circumferential radius is $R e^{-\psi_\Sigma}$, where $\psi_\Sigma$ is the common value of $\psi$ on the shell.
Magnitude of each particle's conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass, a positive length.
Conserved rest mass per unit axial Killing length; the rest mass per proper axial length is $\Lambda = \lambda e^{-\psi_\Sigma}$.

coordinates.convention: We use the independent regional time $t$ and the canonical radius $\rho$, with $g_{\phi\phi}g_{zz}=\rho^2$. The shell is $\rho=R(t)$.

coordinates.name: Cylindrical Exterior

parameters.description: Dimensionless cylindrical wave amplitude; the vacuum wave equation is $\partial_t^2\psi = \partial_\rho^2\psi + \partial_\rho\psi/\rho$. At equilibrium, $\psi=-\kappa\ln(\rho/R_0)$ and $\gamma=\gamma_0+\kappa^2\ln(\rho/R_0)$, where $R_0$ is the equilibrium radius, $\kappa=2\alpha^2/R_0^2$, $\gamma_0=2\ln(1+2\alpha^2/R_0^2)$, and $\lambda=\alpha^2R_0\sqrt{R_0^2+\alpha^2}/(R_0^2+2\alpha^2)^2$.
Canonical radius of the shell at the regional time $t$; its circumferential radius is $R e^{-\psi_\Sigma}$, where $\psi_\Sigma$ is the common value of $\psi$ on the shell.
Magnitude of each particle's conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass, a positive length.
Conserved rest mass per unit axial Killing length; the rest mass per proper axial length is $\Lambda = \lambda e^{-\psi_\Sigma}$.

coordinates.convention: We use the independent regional time $t$ and the canonical radius $\rho$, with $g_{\phi\phi}g_{zz}=\rho^2$. The shell is $\rho=R(t)$.

coordinates.name: Intrinsic Shell

parameters.description: Canonical shell radius as a function of the proper time $\tau$ of observers with fixed $\phi$ and $z$.
Common value of the bulk wave amplitude at the shell, $\psi=\psi_\Sigma$; the induced metric is continuous across the surface.
Magnitude of the conserved particle angular momentum per rest mass; $u=\alpha e^\psi/R$ is the magnitude of the specific azimuthal momentum.

Conserved rest mass per unit Killing length. In an orthonormal shell frame, $S_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,p,0)$, with $\sigma=\lambda\sqrt{1+u^2}/(2\pi R)$ and $p=\lambda u^2/(2\pi R\sqrt{1+u^2})$.

coordinates.convention: We use $(\tau,\phi,z)$ on the material surface; $\tau$ is the proper time of observers with fixed $\phi$ and $z$. The tensors are intrinsic to this surface.
